The paper was published on February 12, 2015, in Mathematical Methods in the Applied Sciences.
The adaptive multiscale moment method (AMMM) was originally developed to solve Fredholm integral equations before being applied to scattering problems.
Breaking sea waves are modeled starting from solitary wave solutions with initial amplitude A = 0.18 m in the presented example.
Standard method of moments requires resolution finer than λ/100 for breaking waves, compared to λ/10 for smooth surfaces.
The hydrodynamic model uses conformal transformations including Schwartz-Christoffel, Kármán-Trefftz, Theodorsen-Garrick, and Cayley-type transformations.
The velocity potential is expressed as a sum of N Rankine sources (Green's functions) located outside the fluid domain.
Sources are positioned using a desingularized technique to ensure mass and energy conservation.
The free surface elevation of a solitary wave is given by η_o(x) = A sech²(b(x-x_s)) with b = √(3A/4h³).
The solitary wave velocity is C = √(g(h+A)), where g = 9.81 m/s² and h is water depth.
Two electromagnetic polarization cases are analyzed: transverse magnetic (TM) and transverse electric (TE).
The 2D Green's function of the Helmholtz equation is used for electromagnetic modeling.
At zeroth scale, N+1 equally spaced nodal points are used with triangular basis functions.
At first scale, one midpoint is added, creating basis functions that span two scales.
At second scale, two additional midpoints are added at positions 1/4 and 3/4, creating five basis functions total.
The multiscale basis functions at order J are linearly related to triangular basis functions through transformation matrices T_J.
The recursive midpoint division process generalizes to any Jth scale by introducing points x_{J,i} = (i-1)/(2^J) for i = 1,2,...,2^J-1.
The coefficients £_{J,i} represent the difference between the function value at scale J and the lower-order approximation.
The linear system from AMMM has a block structure that allows recursive solution using iterative solvers.
The generalized minimal residual method (GMRES) is used as the iterative solver in the implementation.
The iterative solver starting points are always in the basin of attraction of the solution, ensuring quick convergence.
Plunging breaking waves necessarily induce cavities and local curvatures that challenge standard numerical methods.
The peak of local curvature occurs near the plunging wave crest, as shown in Figure 6 of the paper.
Hybrid approaches combining MoM with ray theory and asymptotic approximation have been previously investigated but provide only partial solutions.
Higher-order MoM has been explored as an alternative but is less effective than the multiscale approach.
The paper demonstrates that AMMM is particularly effective for surfaces with high local curvatures and can be applied to arbitrary parametric curves in 2D.
